CoreelementRequest.description:
Superset request body holding every possible field (ignored by the
types that don't use it). Which fields are required/forbidden
and name/label uniqueness all vary by CoreelementType and are checked
in coreelement_service against COREELEMENT_CONFIG, since they depend on
`element_type` -- a sibling *path* parameter the request body itself
has no access to, not expressible as a static Field constraint here.

Length bounds below are a best-effort outer safety net, not the
precise per-type source of truth (that remains COREELEMENT_CONFIG):
`name`'s max varies by type (60 for five types, 16 for Role alone) --
60 is used here as the loosest bound that still rejects clearly
invalid input, so a 17-60 character Role name still passes this layer
and is correctly rejected by the service's own type-specific check.
The four extra fields are each used by exactly one type, so their
bounds here ARE each type's exact, real constraint.
CoreelementRequest.title: CoreelementRequest

ScoreRequest.description:
All 94 score card fields. The form always submits the full card, so
every field must be present in the payload. Blank optional text/select
values (submitted as "") are normalized to None and stored as NULL;
numbers default to 0 in the form and stay required, except
geboren/gestorben/jahr, which stay NULL when left blank -- there is no
meaningful year 0, so unlike every other number field they carry no
"empty means 0" convention (see score_service.py's get_defaults()).

Text is stripped before its length is checked, so a required field made
of blanks counts as empty and no field stores surrounding whitespace.
The setting only touches string values.
ScoreRequest.title: ScoreRequest

post.description:
Hands an immediate Koofr backup, independent of the daily scheduled
job, to the worker container. The web process never runs backups
itself, so it needs neither the Koofr credentials nor the PostgreSQL
client tools, and a long dump cannot hit the request timeout; the
outcome is the `last_run` of the `backup_koofr` job. Production-only:
the shared Koofr path holds one backup history across every stage.
Enforced here (409, avoiding a misleading failed run) AND independently
inside run_backup() itself, so scripts/backup_db.py and the scheduled
job stay protected even without going through this endpoint.

Hands an immediate downsync, independent of the nightly scheduled
job, to the worker container; the outcome is the `last_run` of the
`downsync` job. Unlike trigger_backup, the production gate here is a
REAL security boundary, not just UI convenience: a production downsync
would replace the live database with an older snapshot (real data loss
since the last backup), so it's enforced server-side (409) rather than
only hidden in the frontend.

get.description:

job_runs table.

Always responds 200 regardless of whether the email is registered
-- prevents account enumeration. No auth/permission dependency

post.description:
Direct login via an existing Google binding. Uses Google Identity
Services' ID-token ("credential") flow rather than a server-side OAuth
redirect/callback dance, which would need a session-stored CSRF `state`
that doesn't cleanly exist in a stateless-JWT backend.

Checks the local e-mail and password, so it shares the login lockout
and audit trail: otherwise it would be a way to guess passwords that
the login throttle never sees.

Authenticate with email + password, receive a JWT access token plus
an httponly refresh cookie.

"Anmeldedaten unbekannt." covers BOTH unknown email and wrong password
(the login fails generically for both, which prevents account
enumeration -- there is no separate "Passwort falsch." message in the
login flow, that string belongs to the unrelated self-service
change-password form). Lockout: 5 failed attempts / 60s per e-mail and
address, 20 / 15 min per e-mail from any address, see
auth_service.check_login_throttle.
Invalidate the current session and clear the refresh-token cookie.

post.description:
Exchange the refresh-token cookie for a new access token, rotating
the refresh secret on every use. Per-IP rate limit only.

Answers every registration alike, so an anonymous visitor cannot learn
whether an address or a name is already in use (the login and reset flows
avoid the same enumeration). A new address gets its account, the
verification mail and, in the background, the disponent notice; no session
is issued, the verification link logs in. An address that has an account,
or a name that is taken, creates nothing and gets a mail saying so.
Registration itself must not wait on (or fail because of) mail delivery.
No auth/permission dependency exists on this endpoint (it must work
logged-out), so there is no dependency-ordering concern here, unlike
resend_verification_email below.

Re-sends the verification mail. Deliberately uses get_current_user,
not get_verified_user -- an unverified user must be able to reach
exactly this endpoint. Idempotent: no-op (still 200) if already
verified. current_user is declared BEFORE job_queue on purpose, see
get_job_queue.
